pages.text: The Brain and the Senses

image.note: Cover: a friendly brain, senses radiating

pages.text: Contents. The Control Centre / Sending Messages / The Five Senses / Making Sense of It All / Memory and Sleep / Looking After Your Brain.

Right now, without being told, something inside your head is reading these words, hearing them in a quiet voice, keeping you breathing, and holding you upright in your chair, all at once. You are meeting the most astonishing object in the known universe. It is inside your own skull.

It weighs about as much as a small pineapple, and looks a little like a grey, wrinkled walnut. It has no moving parts. Yet it can imagine a dragon, remember your fifth birthday, and learn to read, which is exactly what it is doing this very second.

image.note: A brain beside a walnut, for scale

pages.text: Think of your body as a busy country, and your brain as its capital city, where every important decision is made. Nothing happens, no step, no word, no blink, without a message to or from the brain.

image.note: Body as a country, brain as capital

pages.text: The brain sits safe inside the hard case of your skull, cushioned in fluid so it does not knock about. It is precious, and the body guards it well. It is greedy too: though it is small, it drinks up huge amounts of the blood and energy your body makes, even while you sleep.

How busy is your brain? It has billions of tiny cells, many times more than there are people on earth, and each one can talk to thousands of others. Laid end to end, the wiring inside your head would stretch for thousands of kilometres. All of it, folded away, inside your skull.

Different parts of the brain do different jobs. A great wrinkled outer layer does your thinking, your talking, and your deciding. A small part at the back keeps you balanced and smooths your movements. And deep inside, older parts quietly run your breathing and heartbeat without ever asking you.

The wrinkles matter. If you could iron your brain's outer layer flat, it would be surprisingly large, far too big for your skull. So it folds and crumples to fit, like a big sheet packed into a small box. More folds mean more room for thinking.

Here is a strange truth. The left half of your brain mostly controls the right side of your body, and the right half controls the left. Wave your right hand, and it is the left side of your brain giving the order. Your control centre works in a mirror.

Try something now. Without looking, touch the tip of your nose with one finger. Easy, was it not? You did not have to see your nose or your finger. Your brain keeps a perfect map of where every part of your body is, all the time, even in the dark.

image.note: Child touching nose with eyes closed

pages.text: For your brain to run a whole body, its messages must travel, fast. They race along a living cable called the spinal cord, which runs down inside your backbone, and branch out along nerves to every corner of you, right to your fingertips and toes.

These messages are tiny bursts of electricity, leaping from cell to cell. They are astonishingly quick. Touch something hot and the news reaches your brain, and the order to pull back races out, in a fraction of a single second.

You can measure how fast your reactions are. Have a friend hold a ruler straight down, your fingers open at the bottom. When they drop it, snatch it. How far it falls before you catch it shows your reaction time, the tiny gap between seeing and doing. Practise, and watch it shrink.

Some messages are so urgent they do not even wait for the brain. Touch a flame, and your spinal cord orders your hand back before your brain has even felt the pain. We call this a reflex: the body's emergency shortcut, built to save you before you can think.

You can feel your reflexes at work. That knee that kicks when a doctor taps it. That blink when something darts at your eyes. You did not decide to do those things. Your body decided for you, faster than thought.

image.note: Doctor tapping a knee, leg kicks

pages.text: Here is why reflexes must be so fast. A message to your brain and back feels instant, but it still takes a little time to travel. If your hand had to wait for your brain every time, you would be burned before you let go. So for true emergencies, the body built a shortcut, and it may have saved your skin more than once.
So your brain and nerves form one vast messaging network, always busy, always talking, carrying millions of messages every second, whether you are running a race or fast asleep.
Your brain sits locked in the dark of your skull. It has never seen the world directly. Everything you know of the world outside, it learns through your senses: your windows onto everything.

image.note: Senses as windows into a dark room

pages.text: Your eyes catch light and turn it into signals your brain can read. And here is a wonder: the picture that lands inside your eye is actually upside down. Your clever brain flips it the right way up so smoothly that you never, ever notice.

image.note: Eye with an upside-down image inside

pages.text: Every eye has a tiny blind spot, a place where it cannot see at all, where the nerve leaves for the brain. You never notice it, because your brain quietly paints over the gap with a guess. In a small way you are being gently fooled by your own brain every waking second, and it is doing it to help you.

image.note: Diagram of the eye's blind spot

pages.text: Your ears catch sound, which is really the air itself trembling. Deep inside your ear, tiny parts shiver with each tremble and turn it into signals. Your brain reads those signals as a voice, a song, or a warning shout.

image.note: Cross-section of an ear, sound waves

pages.text: Your nose and tongue work as a team. Your tongue senses only a few basic tastes, sweet, salty, sour, bitter. Most of what you call "taste" is really smell. That is why, with a blocked nose, even your favourite food tastes of almost nothing.

Prove it at snack time. Pinch your nose shut, close your eyes, and have someone give you a piece of apple, then a piece of pear. Chew. Can you even tell which is which? With your nose blocked, most people cannot. Almost all of what we call taste was smell all along.

Your skin is your largest sense organ of all, wrapped around your whole body, feeling heat, cold, pressure, and pain. It is always on guard. It is why a gentle touch can comfort you, and why a sharp one makes you leap.

Try this with a friend. Close your eyes and have them gently touch your back with one fingertip, or with two held close together. Can you tell how many? On your fingertips you would know at once, but on your back it is much harder. Your skin has far more sensors where you need them most: your hands.

image.note: Two-point touch test on the back

pages.text: Here is a puzzle your senses solve. Why can you not tickle yourself? Because your brain already knows your own hand is coming, and expects it. A tickle needs surprise. Your brain cannot surprise itself, so the giggle never comes.

Your senses only gather. It is your brain that understands. Signals pour in from eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and skin, and the brain weaves them, in an instant, into one smooth world that feels perfectly real and perfectly ordinary.

image.note: Five streams flowing into the brain

pages.text: And your brain does more than report the world. It guesses. It fills in gaps, predicts what comes next, and sometimes it guesses wrong. That is what an optical illusion is: a picture that fools your brain into seeing something that is not there.

Your brain hates a gap, and will always fill it. Read this quickly: your brain can raed wrods with the letetrs jumbled, as long as the first and last are right. You are not really reading the letters at all. You are guessing whole words, faster than you can think, and almost always getting them right.

Your brain also chooses what to ignore. Right now you can feel your socks on your feet, but a moment ago you had forgotten them entirely. Your brain quietly hushed that signal so you could think. It filters the flood, and lets through only what matters.

This is why two people can stand in the same room and notice completely different things. Your brain builds your own private version of the world, from the pieces your senses send it. No two people's worlds are ever quite the same.

This is worth remembering when you argue. Two people can watch the very same thing and honestly, truly see it differently, because each brain built its own picture. Neither is lying. Understanding that other people live in their own version of the world is one of the wisest things your brain can learn to do.

image.note: Two children, same scene, two pictures

pages.text: One of the brain's greatest powers is memory: the ability to keep the past and carry it with you. Your memory holds your name, your friends, the way home, and this very sentence, long enough to reach its end.

image.note: Memories as a shelf of moments

pages.text: Not all memories are the same. Some last only seconds, a phone number you hold just long enough to dial, then let go. Others last a lifetime. The more you use a memory, the stronger it grows, which is exactly why practising a thing makes you better at it.

Here is a memory trick as old as the Greeks. To remember a list, picture each thing in a place you know well: a banana on your front step, a clock in the hallway, a fish on your bed. Walk through the house in your mind, and the pictures leap back to you. Your memory holds pictures and places far better than plain words.

image.note: Memory palace: objects around a house

pages.text: And this is where sleep comes in. Sleep is not the brain switching off. Far from it. While you sleep, your busy brain sorts through your day, keeping what matters, clearing away what does not, and filing your memories away for keeping.

This is why cramming all night before a test can backfire. Rob your brain of sleep, and you rob it of the very hours it uses to file away what you learned. Study, then sleep, and let your brain do its quiet night's work. Sometimes the laziest-looking thing, sleep, is really the brain working hardest.

That is why a good night's sleep helps you remember what you learned, and why tired brains are forgetful and slow. If you want to remember something for a test, sleep may help you more than one more hour awake. Your brain does its filing at night.

Dreams happen in sleep too, when your resting brain stitches stray thoughts and memories into strange little stories. No one is quite sure why we dream. It is one of the many mysteries still hiding inside your own head.

Your brain never truly rests, not even in the deepest sleep. It keeps your heart beating, your lungs breathing, and your body turning so you do not grow stiff. The one thing that runs your whole life is the one thing that never, ever clocks off. It is working for you right now, and it always will.

Your brain is not fixed. It changes, every day, with everything you do. Each time you learn something, real connections form and strengthen inside it. In a true and physical way, learning reshapes your brain. You are rebuilding it as you read.

The best gift you can give your brain is to use it and stretch it: reading, puzzles, music, new skills, hard questions. A brain, a little like a muscle, grows stronger with exercise. This whole book has been a workout for yours.

There is wonderful news hidden in all of this. Because your brain grows with use, no one is simply clever, or not clever, for ever. A brain that struggles with a thing today, and keeps trying, physically builds the wiring to master it. The words you want are not "I can't". They are "I can't yet".

It needs care too. It needs good food and water, for it is a hungry, thirsty thing. It needs plenty of sleep, to do its nightly filing. It needs exercise and fresh air, which send it rich, clean blood. And it needs its hard case protected, which is why we guard our heads.

Sometimes brains are hurt or ill, and doctors who study the brain work to understand and heal them. There is still so much we do not know. Your brain may be the last great unexplored country, and it is riding inside your own head.

image.note: A kind doctor studying a brain scan

pages.text: For all we have learned, the brain guards deep secrets still. We do not fully know how it stores a single memory, or why we dream, or how it turns tiny crackling signals into the feeling of being you. The greatest mystery in all of science may be the very thing reading this sentence.

So here is the wonder to carry away. The thing that read this book is the very thing the book was about. Your brain just spent all these pages learning about itself, and grew a little as it did. Nowhere in all the universe have we yet found anything as marvellous as the object between your ears.

Words to know. Brain: the body's control centre. Nerve: a cable that carries messages. Spinal cord: the great nerve down your back. Reflex: an automatic action. Senses: how the body learns about the world. Memory: the power to keep the past.
Your brain runs a whole astonishing body: a heart, lungs, bones, and blood, all working together this second. Each one has its own story. Which part of your amazing self will you explore next?
